items.title: Polaroid releases new cameras and film to mark 30 years of Pokémon
items.content:
Polaroid has announced its biggest special edition yet to mark the 30th anniversary of the Japanese video game and trading card franchise Pokémon.

Polaroid is releasing no less than three Pokémon-branded Polaroid cameras, along with three special-edition films and three different accessories.

The camera line-up includes two full-sized Now Gen 3 camera, as well as a smaller Go Gen 3 camera.

The different cameras are:

  • Special edition Now Gen 3 – Pokémon design in red, white and black
  • Special edition Go Gen 3 – Pikachu design in yellow and black
  • Special edition Go Gen 3 – Sylveon design in blue, white and pink

The Pokémon camera costs £129.99 in the UK, $139.99 in the US and €139.99 in the EU. The Pikachu and Sylveon cameras cost £89.99 in the UK, $99.99 in the US and €99.99 in the EU.

The three new films are all include Pokémon frames and are as follows:

  • Polaroid Color i-Type Film – Pokémon Edition: (£21.99/$22.99 /€21.99)
  • Polaroid Go Color Film – Pokémon Pikachu Edition – Double Pack: (£21.99/$24.99 €22.99)
  • Polaroid Go Color Film – Pokémon Sylveon Edition – Double Pack: £21.99 / $24.99/€22.99)

The cameras and films are joined by a case, a branded photo album and a special Pokémon strap.

All the new Pokémon-branded products are expected to be available from 25 August.

Polaroid said in a press release: “Celebrating 30 years of Pokémon, the collection marks Polaroid’s biggest collaboration yet and includes three cameras, three film frames with custom dark slides and iconic accessories.

“The products have been designed to bring Pokémon’s playful energy to Polaroid’s iconic cameras, while encouraging both younger and older fans of Pokémon to embrace the tactile, analogue joy of shooting with Polaroid.”

“Pokémon has always been about discovery, connection, and exploration. Working with Polaroid feels like a natural extension of these values: encouraging fans to capture moments that matter most to them in their own way and turn their favourite memories into tangible keepsakes,” said Mathieu Galante, The Pokémon Company International’s senior director of licensing.

items.title: Kosmo Foto’s Direktor walk with the Photographer’s Gallery Bookshop
items.content:
In May, Kosmo Foto originally planned with the help of the Photographer’s Gallery Bookshop to unveil our latest film.

Kosmo Foto Direktor is a limited-edition re-rolled version of Eastman Kodak’s peerless 5222 XX black-and-white cinema film which has been used in iconic films such as ‘Raging Bull’, ‘Casino Royale’ and ‘Oppenheimer’.

Kosmo Foto was released in time for the Photographica camera fair in London in May.

The walk had to be postponed in May, but is now taking place this Saturday (22 August). The Direktor walk will be the only photo walk featuring this film. It will be starting at The Photographers Gallery on Ramilles Street at 11am.

Tickets cost £20 including VAT. Each ticketholder will get a roll of Direktor – which is not available in the shops and can only be ordered from Kosmo Foto.

The walk will work its way through central London visiting various landmarks from cinema history – and we’re challenging you to think like a director, taking shots you think could be stills from a film.

There will also be some spot prizes from Kosmo Foto and its online camera shop Cameraburo.

A note on Direktor: we had originally planned to follow the original version of Kosmo Foto Direktor with further batches in a metal canister, but the cost of producing the film was slightly higher than we’d anticipated. We’d prefer to keep our films as affordable as possible, so unless we can find a cheaper method of producing it, this will be the only batch of the film we will produce.

If you can’t make the walk on Saturday and you still fancy shooting it, head to the Kosmo Foto Shop.

items.title: Harman Phoenix has a new look – and a new ISO
items.content:
Harman Technology is reducing the price of its Harman Photo-branded colour negative films and re-releasing the original Phoenix film with an important update.

The repackaged Harman Phoenix will no longer be an ISO 200 film but will be DX coded for ISO 125.

Harman Technology said it had repackaged the film after feedback from photographers who said the film responded better to being shot at a lower ISO.

The new listing on the Harman Photo shop reads:  “Harman Phoenix 125 retains the same characteristics that you loved (or hated) about the original but with a new speed of 125 to reflect how you told us you shoot it.”

According to Harman Technology, the film still shows high contrast and strong, visible grain at this lower ISO, and should be shot accordingly.

It also says that it can be developed in E6 or ECN-2 chemicals as well.

The listing says: “With a DX coded cassette and a box speed of ISO 125, It performs best in good, consistent light and on brighter days or when shooting into the light there is also a possibility of halation.

‘It delivers punchy, vibrant colours although they react differently to different scanners and settings. Getting the exposure right will certainly help to get the best results so we suggest metering for the mid tones to retain shadow or highlight detail (over or under exposure is not Phoenix’s friend)!”

While the price of the new version of the film – also available in 120 – has not yet been made public, film is expected to be available from stockists as early as next week.

Meanwhile, other films such as Phoenix’s follow-up Phoenix II has been reduced in price to just £7.32 in the UK for a 24-shot roll and £9.27 for a 36-frame roll, with further reductions for five-packs and 10-packs of film. The price of 120 film is also being reduced to £7.90 a roll.

Harman Photo’s experimental films, Red and the recently released Switch Azure, are also seeing price reductions.

items.title: Lomography releases 1980s-styled Discomatic version of Lomomatic 110 camera
items.content:
Lomography has launched a spectacularly colourful new version of its Lomomatic 110 compact camera for summer.

The new Discomatic version of the 110-format camera is in a colour scheme of dazzling blue, pink and yellow – looking every inch like something that might have been released in the 1980s.

“Summer’s here and we’re ready to relive the heyday of the disco with the popping new Lomomatic 110 Discomatic,” Lomography said in a press release. “This colourful concoction comes with all the exciting features that have made the Lomomatic 110 a favorite among the Lomography Community. A true statement of style and a creative sidekick for life, everyone loves a little funk!

“Don’t be fooled by its size – this creative companion is bursting with big ideas! It’s a thrilling companion for analogue beginners, the sharpest and most trusted 110

camera for seasoned photographers, and a nostalgic voyage for those yearning for the grand old days of 110 film.

“Opening the door to a world of possibilities with a 23mm Minitar Glass Lens, fully automatic settings, controllable ISO, zone focusing, and interchangeable apertures, it can squeeze into all types of small spaces for crazy Lomographic perspectives. Ready for anything, the Lomomatic 110 captures fragments of life; each frame a glimpse into a spontaneous moment frozen in time, effortlessly transformed into a vibrant memory.”

Like other editions of the Lomomatic 110, the camera’s specifications are:

Film format: 110
Lens focal length: 23mm
Available apertures: Day f/5.6, Night f/2.8
Maximum aperture: f/2.8
ISO: controllable 100, 200 or 400
Shutter speed: Auto (A), Bulb (B)
Focusing: Zone focus
Flash: Manual on or off
Multiple exposures: Unlimited
Tripod socket: No
Battery: 1 × CR2 (1.5 V)

The camera is available to order now and costs £109 in the UK along with its matching flash.

items.title: Analogue aF-1 release delayed due to ongoing tweaks to prototypes
items.content:
The release of the Analogue aF-1 compact camera – which initially was planned to be produced by the end of last year – has been delayed while its developers fine-tune the pre-production prototypes.

In an email sent out to subscribers, its Amsterdam-based creators said the camera was currently in pre-production, but problems identified in prototypes so far have necessitated delays before the camera can go into full production.

Analogue said it would not “share a delivery date” but would send out more updates as improvements were made.

“When we first announced the aF-1, we genuinely believed we could bring it to market much sooner. Looking back now, that simply wasn’t realistic. If we had known then what we know today, we definitely would have planned some things differently, the team, which is led by Ralph Tilon, said in the update.

“Over the past year and a half, we’ve invested far more time, money, and energy than we ever expected. Not because we have to, but because we genuinely want to build a camera that deserves to exist.

“We’ve learned that building a camera has its own schedule,” the update said. “Rather than continuing to move deadlines, we’d rather keep working, keep sharing meaningful progress, and announce a delivery timeline once we’re confident we can stand behind it.”

The aF-1, announced in January 2025, is a compact 35mm camera with Lidar-based autofocus and a sliding front panel like the Olympus XA or Mju-II. The camera features a 35mm f/2.8 lens and an inbuilt lens. It was a surprise announcement alongside other recent new compact cameras such as the Pentax 17 and the Rollei 35AF.

Designed by the team who also run the camera shop Analogue in Amsterdam, the camera is being manufactured in China. The camera is already available to pre-order for €450 (£390/$512), though the latest update makes it clear that there is, as yet, no confirmed release date.

Earlier this year, Analogue had published another update that said delays in production were caused by modifications to the camera’s auto-focusing unit.

Analogue said: “In about two weeks, we’ll be travelling back to China for another engineering review with our manufacturing partner. We’ll continue sharing updates as we move through the next stage of development and pre-production.”

items.title: China Lucky Film’s new Lucky C400 film released at Chinese trade show
items.content:
China Lucky Film’s latest colour film – called Lucky C400 – has apparently been launched at a photography convention in China.

A post on the Reddit forum r/AnalogCommunity by user GabbasClub showed an update from China’s Lucky Film’s account on the Chinese social media platform RedNote, announcing the new 400-ISO film.

The Photo & Imaging Shanghai 2026 launched on Thursday (23 July) and runs until Monday (27 July).

The RedNote post said: “Lucky C400 film has just been released at the Shanghai exhibition. You can grab it onsite or buy online through multiple channels.”

The film is reportedly available for ¥69 ($10.50/£7.85) which includes processing and scanning in China.

There are no details yet on when the film will be available outside China.

China Lucky Film’s European Instagram page has recently posted images taken on the film, which were posted in the last few weeks. They include the portrait taken by Instagram user calvinonfilm which you can see below:

Lucky C400 is the second colour film to emerge from China Lucky Film since the launch of Lucky C200 last year. It is not a relaunched film, but an entirely new emulsion.

News of Lucky C400 first emerged earlier this year, though there were no details on when it would be available.

China Lucky Film’s new colour releases come amid a burst of activity in colour film production from new producers.

Britain’s Harman Technology – which makes Ilford and Kentmere black-and-white films – is now on the second iteration of its Phoenix colour film after launching the first version at the end of 2023.

Optik Oldschool, a lab based in Dusseldorf in Germany, released Opticolour 200 in 2025, a new colour film believed to be Original Wolfen NC200, which had been teased in early 2025.

Last week it emerged Optik Oldschool had become the new owners of the facility which makes it, InovisCoat, and the company that owns the Original Wolfen brand, Filmotec.

items.title: These two new simple cameras are a positive sign for film’s future
items.content:
In the past week, two new film cameras have been announced. They are bright and bold and very much not aimed at the “serious” photographer.

There is, however, no confusion over who they are definitely aimed at – those who probably haven’t shot a roll of film before.

Their target market is those who’ve tired of shooting everything on their phone, and want something more interesting to capture their memories – and who don’t necessarily want to use a disposable.

The first of these new cameras is the Lomography Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera. Half in film format if not in name, this is a tweaked version of the simple, reloadable 35mm camera Lomography first launched back in 2017.

The Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera came already loaded with a roll of Lomography film but it didn’t die when that roll of film was finished. You rewound the film and then loaded it with another roll from Lomography’s staple (or, indeed, from any other film brand).

The camera has been enough of a success for Lomography to occasionally relaunch it loaded with the latest addition to their film range.

The new half-frame version comes with enough film pre-loaded to shoot 40 frames, though it will of course shoot 72 frames with a standard 36-shot roll inside.

What’s more, the camera was offered for a little under £22 in the UK loaded with Lomography’s Lady Grey black-and-white film, and a touch under £25 loaded with its new colour negative film, LomoChrome Classicolor 200.

Just a day after Lomography’s announcement, Reto Project – the Hong Kong company which licenses the Kodak name across various products – announced their latest camera.

The Kodak EC35 is as bare-bones as Lomography’s Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera – manual film advance, single shutter speed and aperture, integral flash – but adds a sliding film cover like you’d find on the cult (and increasingly pricy) Olympus Mju-II.

Reto are very much aiming it at younger photographers. The camera is available in no less than seven different colours – midnight black, vanilla white, butter yellow, lavender, powder blue, blush pink, and avocado green. Reto seem to be sprinkling a touch of the marketing magic they used last year when they released probably the most talked-about camera of 2025, the Kodak Charmera.

Though the Charmera is a digital model, it oozes an analogue aesthetic. Its branding leans heavily on Kodak’s 1980s packaging, and physically it’s a doppelganger for Kodak’s first disposable, the 110-toting Fling. Reto also offered it in a range of styles and colours – in blind-box packaging which meant you didn’t know when version you’d got your hands on until you opened the box.

Some of the Charmera marketing magic seems to have sprinkled on the Kodak EC35. Granted, you know what colour you’re getting before you rip open the packaging, but that range of colours is a simple but effective decisions. The EC35 is seven different cameras, depending which model ticks your colour chart.

And the price? In the UK, a smidgen under £35, the prices of a three-pack of colour film.

The Half-frame Simple Use camera, meanwhile, adds the idiosyncracy of half-frame to one of Lomography’s smartest simple cameras. Half-frame used to be a relic of film photography’s past – in the last few years it has become contemporary again. The Kodak Ektar H35N (another Reto product) appeared just as film prices were on their uppers; the two-for-one format chimed with the frugal times.

When the Pentax 17 – the first new film camera to come from this major Japanese camera producer in nearly two decades – appeared in 2024, half-frame was no longer a half-forgotten format.

Colour film isn’t as hard to find as it was during the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, but it’s expensive enough that it’s no longer an effortless purchase; there will be plenty of people interested in eking out a roll as long as they can. Twice the photos on a roll of film? Hard to say no to.

The Lomography Half-frame’s appearance seems to have been particularly welcomed; an initial review from the UK’s veteran photography magazine Amateur Photographer by John Stapley has been particularly enthusiastic: “I loved having the freedom to experiment without worrying that I was burning through the film too fast.”

Now, the purists might complain that both these cameras are new arrivals in an already crowded field of simple cameras (like the Dubblefilm SHOW, Moment camera, and any number of other cheap Chinese cameras). Others might point out that you can get a used simple camera for much cheaper from a car boot sale or browsing eBay.

Both these views are valid, but they overlook the fact that two established brands think that there’s enough interest in film that it’s worth their time, money and effort to introduce new cameras aimed at an often fast-moving market.

Despite a sizeable increase in digital camera sales over the last 18 months, enough young photographers are swerving digital entirely in their flight from their phones, and choosing to experiment with film. Whether you’re a Lomographer or a Leica lover, that’s good news.

items.title: Optik Oldschool takes ownership of InovisCoat and FilmoTec, the home of Original Wolfen films
items.content:
German film producer Optik Oldschool has been revealed as the new owner of InovisCoat and FilmoTec.

InovisCoat is the coating facility which coats many films for third parties, including Lomography. FilmoTec is the film-producing company that was spun out of the former East German film brand ORWO.

The two companies had recently been under the ownership of British businessman Jake Seal, with FilmoTec’s films being sold under the label “Original Wolfen“.

Optik Oldschool said in a blog post on Wednesday (22 July): “We are incredibly proud to announce that Optik Oldschool’s co-founder Chris Vandebroek has acquired InovisCoat (Monheim) and FilmoTec/Original Wolfen (Wolfen, Bitterfeld).

“With this acquisition, we are no longer just developing and distributing photographic film. The Optik Oldschool family has become a film manufacturer.

“This is about far more than business.

“It is about preserving one of Europe’s most important centres of photographic film production and ensuring that film Made in Germany continues to have a future. At a time when manufacturing is increasingly being moved abroad, we have chosen the opposite path: to protect knowledge, safeguard jobs and preserve decades of expertise.”

Optik Oldschool initially started as a film lab in Dusseldorf in Germany in 2024, and started film production the following, when it launched the colour film Opticolour 200. This was widely believed to be the same film as the Original Wolfen NC200 which had been unveiled at The Photography Show in London in March 2025, but which was never commercially launched.

The film was initially launched in 35mm and 120 formats, but has also been released as a 4×5 film.

Since the launch of Opticolour 200, Optik Oldschool also took over the Santa Film brand which had been owned by Camera Rescue in Finland, and has restarted production of its Santa Color 100 and Santa Color 800 films.

As recently as last week, it also unveiled a new black-and-white film under the Optik Oldschool brand, called OptiMono 100.

Optik Oldschool said negotiations to take over the business, both part of Seal’s portfolio, started last year. “During the summer of 2025, discussions about the acquisition began and were successfully concluded in July 2026.”

The news comes after months of speculation over Seal’s continued ownership of the Original Wolfen brand, which had been dogged by problems with fulfilling customer orders.

German film photography magazine Silvergrain Classics published a story on Wednesday about the new change of ownership, saying: “With the acquisition of InovisCoat, Optik Oldschool gains control of one of the very few companies in the world capable of developing modern photographic emulsions and coating them in multiple layers. The addition of Filmotec brings decades of expertise in the manufacture of photographic and motion-picture films.”

items.title: Reto Project launches new beginner’s film camera called the Kodak EC35
items.content:
Reto Project has released a new Kodak-branded 35mm film camera aimed at beginners called the Kodak EC35.

The camera is a simple point-and-shoot featuring manual advance and with an inbuilt flash.

The new camera was announced on Friday (17 July) and is already available to order. It has a recommended price of just £35 in the UK and $34.99 in the US.

One feature the new camera shares with much more expensive and well-specified retro compacts like the Olympus Mju-II is a sliding front panel.

Reto Project said in the new camera’s listing: “The Kodak EC35 is a beginner-friendly point-and-shoot camera that strips away the complexity of film photography, putting the pure joy back into every frame. Featuring a tactile slide cover for instant protection and a built-in flash, it’s designed to be tossed in your bag and ready for every golden moment!”

The Kodak EC35 has a 25mm two-element f/10 acrylic lens and a fixed shutter speed of 1/100. The internal automatic flash is powered by a single AA battery.

The camera looks to be marketed specifically to younger users, and is being released in no less than seven different colours: midnight black, vanilla white, butter yellow, lavender, powder blue, blush pink, and avocado green.

The new camera is also being offered in a starter kit bundled with a roll of Kodak Ultramax 400-ISO colour film.

You can see some example pics taken on the Kodak EC35 below:

The new camera’s release comes after Reto Project launched other very popular Kodak-branded camera aimed at the younger end of the photography market.

Though a digital camera, the Kodak Charmera, launched in 2025,has leaned heavily on the aesthetic appeal of Kodak’s heritage branding. It’s diminutive design was also based on Eastman Kodak’s first disposable camera, the 110-format Kodak Fling.

Last year, it also released the Snapic A1, a 35mm compact camera featuring a two-element glass lens and motorised film advance.

items.title: Lomography launches half-frame versions of the Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera
items.content:
Lomography has released new half-frame versions of its popular Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera.

Two versions of the new half-frame 35mm camera were announced on Wednesday (15 July), one loaded with LomoChrome Classicolor 200 colour negative film, and the other loaded with Lomography’s or Lady Grey black-and-white film.

Lomography said in a press statement: “Our beloved Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera family is gaining a new member! The Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera is now available in two editions, ready to create more memories, more photos and more madness on 35 mm film.

“Preloaded with 40 photos on LomoChrome Classicolor film or Lady Grey Black & White film, it’s ready to shoot straight out of the box, with a built-in flash and three interchangeable coloured gel filters on the colour edition. Once it’s done, it’s easier than ever to reload and shoot all the way to 72 frames!”

The original versions of the Simple Use Reloadable, which offers the ease-of-use of a disposable with the option to reload and shoot again, was originally launched in 2017.

Lomography followed it up with a new version pre-loaded with the new LomoChrome Classicolor 200 film last year.

Lomography said “Portable and ready for anything – this pocket-sized Simple Use Reloadable camera shoots undeniably analogue snaps in the half-frame format! Made for street, action and creative photography, this new addition to our much-loved family of Simple Use cameras can be re-used endlessly for one-of-a-kind snapshots of life as it happens.”

The two new half-frame cameras are already available to order from the Lomography Shop, with the colour version costing £24.90 in the UK and the black-and-white version costs £21.90.

items.title: KONO! releases three new experimental colour films
items.content:
German film brand KONO! has released three new experimental colour films.

All three films feature strong colour casts and are called Mojo, Offbeat and Bebop.

KONO said in a press release: “KONO! Mojo is the boldest addition to the line-up. Featuring strong colour shifts, deep contrast, and an energetic visual character, it transforms everyday scenes into expressive, graphic images. From vibrant street photography and nightlife to festivals, fashion, and experimental projects, KONO! Mojo is made for photographers who want every frame to stand out.

“With KONO! OffBeat, colour follows its own path. Inspired by the character of cross-processed film, it introduces rich emerald greens and cyan tones while preserving the natural qualities of available light. The result is a distinctive yet versatile film that delivers vivid, unconventional images for travel, portraits, street photography, and everyday creative work.

“Completing the trio is KONO! Bebop, a refined film that embraces subtlety and atmosphere. Its elegant tonal depth, gentle colour palette, and balanced contrast create calm, cinematic images with a timeless analogue aesthetic. Whether photographing landscapes, architecture, portraits, or quiet everyday moments, Bebop offers a sophisticated visual signature that rewards careful observation.”

The films were announced on 7 July and are already available from the KONO! online store. All cost €17.90 (£15.25/$20.40) per roll, or can be purchased as a bundle of all three emulsions for €45.60 (£38.85/$51.95).

The new KONO! films come on the heels of two recent experimental films from Harman Technology, who have adapted their first colour film – Haman Phoenix – to create the redscale Red and the turquoise-toned Switch Azure.

Meanwhile, China’s Reflx Lab has recently unveiled Diablo 100, a redscale film adapted from another recent colour negative release, China Lucky Film’s Color 200.

items.title: Single Frame: Nuns at the doorway
items.content:
The received wisdom of street photography is that your subject has to be front on.

Want your subject to connect with the viewer? You need to see their eyes. It’s how we interact with our fellow humans, reading the emotions and intent on their faces.

Well, like all good rules, this is one that’s made to be broken.

In early 2024, I headed to the Canary Islands for 10 days for some winter sun, including several days on Tenerife and La Palma.

March in the Canaries was much warmer than the dying days of an English winter but definitely still in the sleepy end of their tourist season. There was plenty to explore, and a minimum of packed crowds to push through to do it.

La Palma’s capital Santa Cruz de La Palma is a pint-sized harbour capital of about 20,000 people; first founded in the 15th Century, it has endured everything from pirate sackings to agricultural collapse, and always managed to cling on. You can walk right around its compact centre in under an hour, the roaring Atlantic crashing against the shore.

Santa Cruz de La Palma’s streets are not London’s Oxford Street, nor New York’s Fifth Avenue, but a street is a street, and even the smallest can present you with a photo opportunity if you have your eyes open.

These nuns appeared in a street not too far from the city’s beach, almost hidden under their tunics and habits. They moved slowly and steadily towards a door, knocked on it – and the door opened. The woman answering it was perfectly framed to their left, a quizzical expression on her face.

I had just enough time to rattle off a shot on the camera in my hand – a Ricoh FF-700, a chunky compact camera from the mid-1980s. The Ricoh has a giant LCD screen that takes up virtually all of its top plate and has a decidedly grunty film advance. It also has a superb f/2.8 lens, and I’ve found it a fantastic camera for street photography.

Street photography purists might baulk at having a camera like this – we’re told that ultra-quiet rangefinders are the best tool, because they don’t signal that we’re taking a photo and the subjects remain natural.

When your subject has their back turned on the other side of the street, however, it doesn’t really matter.

items.title: Reflx Lab adds colour 110 films to line-up
items.content:
Chinese photographic brand Reflx Lab has launched two new films in a format that until recently was almost extinct: 110.

It means the company is now one of only two film producers – alongside Lomography – that produce film in this format.

Reflx Lab has started with two colour films – a 110 version of China Lucky Film’s Lucky 200 colour negative film (Fortuna C200), and Kodak Ektachrome 100D (100R) slide film.

The Shenzhen-based company has created its own canisters from scratch and said it was looking at adding more films to the line-up.

“Making 110 film was actually a happy accident!” co-founder Yongxiang told Kosmo Foto, saying it was a side-project from the company’s production of another defunct format, 127. “It started when we began producing 127 film on our own. We were cutting down 120 film (61.5mm) to 127 size (46mm), which left us with a bunch of 16mm-wide leftovers.

“We hate wasting film, so we thought: why not try making 110? It turned out to be way easier than we thought.”

Yongxiang said Reflex Lab tested the waters by purchasing a number of 110 cameras “We had a blast and totally fell in love with the format. 110 cameras are cheap and wonderfully pocketable, and the results have that gorgeous, gritty grain you can’t get anywhere else. Plus, rolling 16mm film into 110 cassettes by hand makes it super budget-friendly.”

He added the biggest challenge “was the cassettes. An injection mould can cost upwards of $5,000, which just wasn’t worth it for a small team like ours. Instead, we used 3D printing and did a ton of light-leak testing. To keep the respooling process simple, we also decided to ditch the backing paper entirely. We removed the little clear window from the back of the cassette so the film wouldn’t get exposed. The downside? No frame counter. But honestly, we don’t think it matters much.

“Right now, we have two 110 films available: Lucky 200 (colour negative) and Ektachrome (slide film). Lucky C200 is made from our 120-to-127 leftover strips, so the film stock is basically free. Ektachrome is my absolute favourite, and since 35mm Ektachrome is getting so expensive and hard to find, we wanted a fun way to shoot it.”

Fortuna C200 costs $19.99 (£12.70) for a pack of three 24-frame films, while a three-pack of 100R costs $24.99 (£18.65).

Reflx Lab has posted examples taken on the new films. Below is a gallery of images taken on Fortuna C200:

And below are some sample images taken on the 100R slide film:

Yongxiang aid Reflx Lab had built a custom trimmer to slit 120 film into rolls of 127 and  110, as well as another trimmer that cuts one 120 roll into four separate rolls of 110 film.

“For Ektachrome, we just use standard 16mm film, which is super easy. Next up, we’re planning to release Double-X and Verita!”

Yongxiang said that the decision to make 110 film aligned with Reflx Lab’s broader strategy to [produce films across various formats, and not just the most popular such as 35mm and 120. “That’s why we’re proudly sticking to 220, 127, and 110,” he said.

items.title: Life after West Yorkshire Cameras: Howard Parker’s new online camera shop
items.content:
It is more 18 months since Leeds camera shop West Yorkshire Cameras closed its doors for good.

The shop had been open for little more than a decade, but in that time had become one of the most popular shops in the UK for those still shooting film.

A few years before film’s second wind really kicked in, founder Howard Parker and his team decided to do something different: concentrate on entirely on analogue. To film fanatics like myself, visiting West Yorkshire Cameras’ website became a daily ritual.

Their prices were fair and their stock accurately described; I never had to send anything back because reality didn’t match the description. Boxes always came with a complimentary bag of Yorkshire Tea or a packet of sweets. Once, realising they were sending something to me, they included a cheap medal awarding me the title of “Supreme Soviet Cameras Collector”(which I still have somewhere, I promise.)

The challenges of keeping a high-street used camera store going amid Brexit, Covid and the financial effects of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, however, took their toll. Parker announced the shop would close its doors in November 2024, and West Yorkshire Cameras was no more.

Now, after a break of 18 months (during which time he got married), Parker has returned to camera selling … though this time it is online rather than on the high street.

Kosmo Foto got some details on the new website, Howard Parker Photographic.

When did you decide to set up the new website?

“Setting up a new photographic venture wasn’t entirely intentional. A few months after closing West Yorkshire Cameras, I had a local customer contact me regarding a very large camera collection, with all manner of equipment. Old, new, digital and analogue. Initially, I wanted to simply help him forward the kit on to the right people. After digging through the collection for a week or so – checking, testing and cataloguing it all – I found my enjoyment of the process returning. I could go at my own pace, and spend time where I might not have been able to before. Cleaning, researching, repairing, and generally having fun with the process again.

“Fast forward a couple of months, and the final count of cameras, lenses and other major accessories was in excess of a thousand. I made the customer an offer for everything, which was accepted. Subsequently, I got in touch with the friends and colleagues in the industry to help move on many of the items, and decided to set up a website to sell some of the nicer pieces myself.”

How is this different to WYC?

“It’s quite different. West Yorkshire Cameras was a much larger operation, and I’d like this to remain smaller and more sensible. Of course, the main difference is that there’s no physical shop. I’m doing all my work from home which feels very refreshing and lets me work at my own pace. In doing so, I am also able to spend more time on customers and individual items. I can provide more detailed condition reports for each item, and more personal service. Now that I have the time, I’m also getting deeper into the intricacies of camera repair. The Yorkshire Tea remains, you’ll be pleased to hear.”

What did you learn from WYC you’ve brought to this?

“First and foremost, I’ve learnt that in a niche interest like analogue photography – it’s all about trust and building connections with customers and colleagues. The support from the community was amazing, both when running West Yorkshire Cameras, and when I announced the closure. I’m in contact with so many amazing people in the photography space because of it, and everyone brings their own individual part.

“Going back to what I’ve personally brought over; quite a bit of time was spent over the years refining the process of assessing, valuing and buying collections of camera equipment. The volume and variety of equipment that the WYC team and I handled through the lifetime of the shop has given me a wide range of knowledge and experience across many camera brands. Whatever kind of system it may be, it’s probably got a plethora of accessories, common issues, collectable aspects or unusual model variations.

“Having said that, every day is absolutely a school day – and that’s part of the fun for me. Never stop learning.”

What kind of gear will you be concentrating on?

“I’d like to keep this more curated and sell a small quantity of equipment which aligns with my own interests. Of course, dealing with high-end Leica, Hasselblad, Rolleiflex etc. is nice – and they always sell well – but I’d also like to have some more esoteric, novelty and collectable items available too. My own collection is a little like that. I might also stock some digital equipment, if the mood strikes.”

How has the analogue camera market changed since you started WYC?

“Way back in 2012, it was certainly different. Both film and equipment were cheaper and more accessible. You could take more risks shooting film. You could throw a roll of AgfaPhoto Vista into your charity shop Olympus Trip 35, absolutely blast through the frames, and take it to Max Spielman for £4 Dev & CD. If there was a problem, you’d spent practically nothing. It didn’t matter as much. You could shoot on vibes. (Do you remember Poundland baskets full of film? Take me back).

“Comparing now to then, I think shooting film is becoming a little more of a refined practice. The cost of a retail roll of film has meant the ‘vibes’ crowd have moved on to digicams (even old phones, I hear) and analogue photography has evolved into a market for dedicated enthusiasts and collectors. As camera enthusiasts, we want to know our cameras are reliable, and our shots are going to come out.

‘The market is changing and I see a lot more homebrew, honest, hardworking camera retailers stepping up to meet these needs. People like Cameras By Max, JFR Film, PPP Repairs, with strong social media presences, are sharing their processes of refurbishing and repairing photographic equipment. I also see more interest in enthusiast-made tools and equipment to keep these cameras going.

“It’s a skill and a community which we will need to foster if we are to keep shooting these ageing cameras. The good news is that those communities are very active, and there are plenty of resources out there if you want to learn.

“Going back to manufacturers of new cameras and lenses, there are many high-quality offerings from independent makers such as Alfie Cameras, Smartflex, TT Artisan and other Chinese Leica clones, which goes to show that dedicated individuals are really stepping up to meet the needs of the market.”

What are some of the highlights you’re offering at the moment?

“Among the stock I have at the moment is a very clean Hasselblad 503CW kit, as well as a pair of Hasselblad Xpan cameras, several lovely black paint Leicas, and a large Portrait Petzval from the late 1800s. I’m always looking to purchase good quality equipment, and am in talks with various customers regarding more items that will hopefully be coming my way soon.”

Is it hard finding quality cameras in the UK compared to a decade ago?

“I would certainly agree with that. Quality equipment is much scarcer now. Even regular equipment – like a ‘Big 5’ SLR – isn’t that easy to find in good condition. The folks that have nice gear, tend to hold onto it. Cameras are being used, ageing and breaking – sometimes irreparably. The nature of reducing supply and increasing interest in analogue (and therefore increased demand) has meant that in general it costs more to buy a good film camera than it used to.

“As mentioned above, the good news is that manufacturers and independent enthusiasts are making new cameras and lenses, which wasn’t happening a decade ago. If anyone industrious out there is reading this, I’d love to help design and bring a new camera to market.”

items.title: Fujifilm marks 40 years of QuickSnap cameras with two new models
items.content:
Fujifilm is marking the 40th anniversary of its QuickSnap disposable cameras with two new models which will be available later this year.

The two models include a new waterproof model and another using black-and-white film.

The underwater Quicksnap Active will be released in early August, with the QuickSnap Black and White scheduled for a September release.

Fujifilm Japan said in a press release: “QuickSnap marks its 40th anniversary in July 2026 and has sold more than 1.7 billion units worldwide to date. Today, its unique characteristics, including the excitement of not knowing how photos will turn out until development and the distinctive, atmospheric quality of the images, continue to resonate with a wide range of users, particularly among younger generations.

“At this milestone, Fujifilm will launch two new products, QuickSnap Active’ and QuickSnap Black and White’, which further expand the range of shooting scenes and creative expressions with QuickSnap.


“The waterproof model QuickSnap Active’ enables underwater photography at depths of up to 10m (33ft). It can be used with ease in a wide range of active scenes, including at the beach or pool, during winter sports, and while camping, allowing users to capture the experience and excitement of the moment as they see it and preserve it in distinctive photographs.

“The QuickSnap Black and White model, featuring black-and-white film, enables users to capture refined black and white images that highlight the subject without the need for special settings or advanced techniques. It allows anyone to easily transform everyday moments into artistic photographs.”

The QuickSnap Black and White model contains film which can be developed in conventional C-41 chemicals, which means that it probably contains Ilford Photo XP2 Super film made by Harman Technology in the UK.

The waterproof QuickSnap Active, meanwhile, features ISO 800 colour film and has an outsized advance knob for operating underwater. It also does not include a flash.

Fujifilm Japan is also releasing a new QuickSnap Hand Strap to attach to the new models, and will release a new logo – resembling a disposable camera – for the QuickSnap range’s anniversary.

items.title: Reflx Lab releases redscale Diablo 100 film
items.content:
Chinese photographic brand Reflx Lab has released a new redscale film called Diablo 100.

The film, which like all redscale films renders images in yellows, oranges and rich reds, is an experimental version of the recently released Lucky 200 colour negative film from China Lucky Film.

On its shop listing, Reflx Lab said: “Reflex Lab Diablo 100 is an experimental film where standard colour film is loaded backward so that light passes through the transparent base before hitting the light-sensitive emulsion. This reverses the order in which colours are exposed, shifting your images to dramatic, fiery shades of red, orange, and yellow.”

The film achieves the characteristic redscale look because the film is essentially reversed in the cassette, with the images are exposed on the emulsion through the base layer, with the red-sensitive layer of the film exposed first instead of last.

Because of the tendency for redscale films to render images almost completely red at their native ISO, Diabolo is rated at ISO 100 instead of Lucky Color 200’s native ISO 200.

The film is available in 36-frame 35mm rolls and can be bought via the Reflx Lab online shop and costs $10.99 a roll.

You can see examples from the film in the gallery below, provided by Reflx Lab, including a shot of how the colours change depending on the ISO setting (click on the images to see a larger version):

The film is the second 35mm redscale film to have appeared in the last 18 months. In February 2025, the UK’s Harman Technology released Red, a reversed version of their first colour film Phoenix.

items.title: Lomography releases summer-themed Fisheye No. 2 La Mer
items.content:
Lomography has announced a new nautically themed edition of its Fisheye No. 2 wide-angle 35mm camera.

The blue-and-sand Lomography Fisheye No. 2 La Mer features the design’s 170° lens and delivers “dreamy bulbous Lomographic snapshots full of vignettes, light leaks and analogue charm”.

Paint the palettes of your portraits during the sunny days or warm summer nights with the built-in flash and get up close and personal with its 10cm closest focusing distance.

“The detachable viewfinder gives you freedom to get lost in the sea of possibilities and trust your instincts on any romanticised escapade. Live freely, love loudly and set sail into any voyage boldly – no matter how the tides change.”

The camera takes characteristic fisheye-style images, with circular images surrounded by elements of the lens housing.

This edition of the camera – which was first released in 2009 – is made of periwinkle-blue plastic with a sand-coloured detachable viewfinder.

It is available to buy now from the Lomography Shop and in the UK costs £69.

The Fisheye No. 2 La Mer’s specifications are:

items.title: Single Frame: Winter courier
items.content:
The pan is one of the simplest photography techniques. Mastering it is one of the quickest ways to elevate your photography.

Rather than keeping the camera still as a moving subject sweeps by, you keep the subject firmly in your view as it moves past. That way you’re rendering the background as a blur, and keeping your subjects still and sharp. Simple, right?

Mastering it is the clincher. I can think of plenty of times I’ve snapped something zooming past me at speed – either from the side of the road or out the window of a train – and then remembered that I wasn’t panning. It’s the simple repeated mistakes that will annoy you.

On this day, at least, I remembered the pan before I clicked the shutter.

This was taken back in January, on a cold, wet winter’s day. I was doing one of my usual weekday routines – snapping off half a roll of film on a commute into the office. I’ve realised that getting one train earlier gives me 45 minutes to wander my way slowly through central London; it’s a good way to keep on top of testing cameras for Cameraburo.

This being cold, grey, wintery London, I’d loaded Ilford Photo XP2 Super into a Canon Sure Shot 76 Zoom. XP2 Super is the last chromogenic black-and-white film on the market – the pictures you get are true black-and-white, but the film is processed in C41 chemicals for colour film. That means you can drop it in to your local minilab along with your colour films. It’s become my go-to film for winter. (The ISO 400 rating certainly helps with UK winter weather too.)

The Canon Sure Shot 76 Zoom is one of the vast Sure Shot range of compact cameras Canon churned out from the early 1980s to the mid-2000s. It’s the kind of camera I would have walked past with barely a glance a decade ago, but very much the kind of camera that flies off the Cameraburo shelves.

And there’s a reason they fly off the shelves: simple to use, just enough creative control to feel like you’re taking a photograph and not just jabbing at a button, a decent lens that doesn’t zoom too far. It’s a bit of a quiet classic that deserves a lot more attention.

And, crucially, the Sure Shot 76 Zoom is the kind of camera that you will fit in your jacket pocket, allowing you to snap spur-of-the-moment shots like this on your way to work. Whether you remember to pan, however, is all down to you.

items.title: The Praktica VF212 reusable camera revives an iconic Cold War name
items.content:
A new film camera has been released bearing the famous East German Praktica brand – but it’s very different to the old-school metal SLRs that once bore the name.

Shops in the UK have begun selling a new simple reusable compact camera with Praktica branding in recent months.

Called the Praktica VF212, the camera is broadly similar to a rash of simple plastic compacts that have appeared in the last decade or so as millennials and Gen Z flock to film.

The camera is showing up in high-street UK retailers such as Curry’s, Boots and Maplin’s.

The VF212 is available in either black or cream, and features a fixed aperture of between f/9 and f/11, a built-in flash and manual film advance and rewind.

The VF212 appears to be typically selling for around £19.99 in the UK.

“Meet your new favourite film companion – the Praktica Reusable 35mm Film Camera. Designed for everyday adventures, this easy-to-use camera brings back the charm of analogue photography with the freedom to reload and shoot again and again,” a listing for the camera on UK pharmacy chain Boots said.

It is not the first film camera in recent years to appear under the Praktica banner.

Kosmo Foto reported in 2024 that a disposable compact under the Praktica name was also being sold in UK high-street store. Called the Luxmedia, the camera came loaded with a roll of 400-ISO colour film. The VF212 requires you to buy film separately.

The camera is, of course, not made in Germany – like the many other simple reusable compacts, it’s a basic China-made model.

It is 25 years since VEB Pentacon – one of the biggest camera makers in East Germany during the Cold War – produced its last German-made Praktica film SLR, the BX20s. The Praktica name, however, lived on with a variety of cheap film and digital models made in Asia during the 2000s and 2010s.

items.title: Light Lens Lab publishes lengthy film update – and still hopes to release film by the end of 2026
items.content:
Chinese lens producer Light Lens Lab has released more detail on its ambitious film production plans.

As previously reported on Kosmo Foto, the company – best known for the Leica-mount lenses – has unveiled plans for a raft of new film products.

In previous posts it has shown ongoing process in its release of its first film, a black-and-white negative film.

In the latest blog update, which was published on Monday (15 June), it also published a roadmap for releasing film in a number of different formats, which include:

  • 120
  • 135
  • 127
  • 126
  • 4×5
  • 8×10

The company also said it was committed to releasing its first film before the end of 2026.

Light Lens lab said: “Since our last development blog, we have continued to make progress on the first iteration of our black-and-white film production line.

“Our current objective is to begin testing our production and assembly workflow in 2026, with the goal of producing our first commercially available black-and-white photographic film in 2026.

Our goal is not only to manufacture black-and-white film but also to establish a complete, internally controlled production system that delivers consistent, high-quality results across multiple photographic formats.

The plans for Light Lens Lab’s film line were first unveiled in January 2025, with initial samples being made public soon after. Public updates have been sporadic since then, thought the company had said it hoped to release film in 2026.

In this week’s update, the company admitted that problems with the stability of the emulsion and other quality control issues had delayed production.

During a test of its 8×10 version of the emulsion, Light Lens Lab said it had identified problems with static electricity build up during the emulsion coating and drying processes, which can seen in the image below:

“As a result, we decided to delay the official release until our production and quality-control processes become more consistent, repeatable, and fully automated,” Light Lens Lab said.

“This is part of the learning process of building a photographic film production system from the ground up at a commercial scale. We cannot allow unresolved quality-control issues to appear in official production. Our objective is to produce a film that meets a high standard of consistency and reliability, without creative or technical compromise.”

The Chinese photographic brand has said that it wants to make sure its film has consistent contrast across different lighting conditions, reliable results with different processing recipes, an ability to be reliable push-processed, and a clean image structure without any production defects.

It said that in the last month it had moved its film production facility into its lens research lab in the Chinese city of Shangrao, allowing them to build a second clean room dedicated to the film project.

Light Lens Lab said it was testing an “automated production system that combines several dedicated machines, including an emulsion coater, master roll splicer, and 135-format film hole puncher” ahead of production.

It added: “Instead of relying on a single universal machine, we are developing specialized coating, slitting, punching, packaging, and assembly systems for each major stage of production.

“This approach allows us to refine each process independently and improve production consistency over time.”

The lengthy update from the company also mentioned that “all machinery, tools, and parts for this project are developed and produced in-house by Light Lens Lab, without partnerships with other companies or third-party manufacturing”.

It added: “Our objective is to build an independent film production platform from the ground up, with full control over design, engineering, production, testing, assembly, and quality control.”

It said it would soon be publishing other blog posts charting progress on some of its other film projects, including an eagerly awaited peel-apart instant film.

items.title: Single Frame: Summer in the City
items.content:
When the City of London’s workers clock off at the end of the week, this hive of financial activity buzzes for a few hours with loud throngs outside the bars and pubs. Then they trickle off to the nearby Tube and train stations. The weekend is two long days of calm.

The City has become something of a mecca for London photographers on the weekends. Monumental architecture of steel and glass catches and reflects the light in pleasing pools. The occasional figures padding past the closed shops help give it human scale.

Increasingly, it’s a place I head to when I have cameras to test for my shop. All that glass and metal creates fantastic backdrops you don’t get in London’s older neighbourhoods.

This day, I was testing a Pentax PC-303. If you’ve never heard of it, don’t worry – it’s not a camera that crops up on many “must-have” lists. Pentax’s PC range of compact cameras started with the flagship (and very impressive) PC-35AF and PC-35AF-M models in the mid-1980s, before morphing into a more budget-minded range in the late 1980s. The PC-303 is pretty typical of them, with a single shutter speed and a switch on the bottom for ISO 100, 200 and 400 films.

Sophisticated it is not, but it’s tougher than a lot of its contemporaries and comes with an excellent 35mm lens. I sell a lot of cameras like this, and I’ve learned to enjoy shooting them for what they are – fuss-free ways to get a photo in good light.

It was also that most important of cameras – the one I had on me at the time. I try to keep a camera like this on me as much as possible. You never know what you might see turning a corner, even if it’s a quick trip to the shops for a pint of milk.

The car was parked on the shady side of the street, the strong sunlight reflecting onto it off the walls behind me. The three figures, engrossed in a conversation I couldn’t hear, anchor the other side of the shot. The cool of the shadows is offset by the bright, stark summer sunlight. It’s the perfect city corner to stumble across with a camera in hand.

items.title: Ultra-rare Swedish military Leica sets high price at Leitz Photographica Auction
items.content:
An almost box-fresh Leica IIIg camera produced for the Swedish military in the 1960s sold for more than three times its estimate at the Leitz Photographica Auction in Germany on the weekend.

The camera, still in its original box and with its original Swedish-language instructions, was one of only 125 of the premium Leica screw-mount model produced in a special batch for Sweden’s armed forces.

Originally estimated to sell for between €140,000 and €150,000 (£121,000 to £129,700/$162,500 to $174,000), the boxed camera ended up selling for €456,000 (£394,000/$529,400) at the sale in Wetzlar, Germany, on Saturday (13 June).

Letiz Photographica Auction said in its listing: “A highly important and exceptionally rare military version of the Leica IIIg, produced in satin black paint for the Swedish Armed Forces and engraved with the distinctive Three Crowns of Sweden on the rear of the top plate.

“Of this special Swedish Army batch, only approximately 125 cameras are recorded (serial range 987901–988025), making it one of the rarest regular-production screw-mount Leicas of the post-war era.

“The present example is preserved in almost New Old Stock condition — an extraordinary state for a military-issued camera. The black paint finish remains beautifully intact, with minimal handling traces and small bubbles appearing in the paint. Swedish Army IIIg cameras were generally issued and used; examples surviving in such remarkable preservation are exceedingly rare, making this a true condition-rarity.”

The sellers noted the lot combined “extreme rarity, outstanding state of preservation, and full original accessories in a manner seldom seen on the market”.

The military IIIg was one of a number of rare military cameras to be offered for sale at this June’s sale.

A one-off Astro-Berlin rifle camera built for the German Luftwaffe during World War II, previously featured on Kosmo Foto, failed to sell, but other popular lots included a rare original Leica MP – one of only 402 – which sold for €600,000 (3518,800/$696,700).

items.title: The Rubin-1: A pioneering Soviet zoom lens from the 1960s
items.content:
By Roman Yarovitsyn

It happened at last! I’ve got into my hands on a Zenit-6 SLR, the dream camera of the character from the Soviet movie ‘Zigzag of Luck’.

In addition to the fact, that it was a most advanced SLR in the USSR (with semi-automatic exposure control), it was equipped with the Rubin-1 lens, the first-ever Soviet zoom lens. Such a fancy camera was just the realms of fantasy for Soviet photographers in 1964, when it released. That’s why Vlad Oreshnikov, who dreamed about a photojournalistic career with this camera went on a rampage and purchased a lottery ticket to launch the plot of  the comedy film ‘Zigzag of Success’.

We must say that Zenit-6 is one of three models, which makes up a family of Soviet SLRs with a leaf shutter. All three released in 1964 and the basic model was the Zenit-4, which was described on Kosmo Foto recently. The Zenit-5 was equipped with electric drive and Zenit-6 was a kit with a Rubin-1 zoom lens instead of the standard Vega-3.

The last model was the most rare: less than 9,000 produced. Technically, the Zenit-6 is identical to the Zenit-4. The only difference is a badge, or more precisely the digit on it: a 6 instead of 4. It looks strange for those who are not familiar with the Soviet photographic market. In the Soviet Union it was not customary to sell a camera body without lens because shortages might mean customers had to wait months for a matching lens.

Nevertheless, a Zenit-E with a Helios-44 or an Industar-50 kept the same name. The Zenit-6 got its name only because the Rubin was so different from the Vega that it forced designers to reconsider the whole kit.

The first Soviet zoom was too bulky and Krasnogorsk Mechanical Plant was forced to change the usual ever-ready camera case to a much bigger case. The Rubin was not only huge, it was also heavy; the shoulder strap attaches not to the camera but to lugs provided on the lens barrel. The weight and price of Zenit-6 were so large, that KMZ felt that it needed to entice the prospective customer with the addition of some small pleasant photographic gifts, such as an interchangeable waist-level viewfinder and colour filters.

Unfortunately, my Zenit-6 body appeared not to work and considering the complete similarity of its earlier cousin, I used my verified Zenit-4 from previous test to check the Rubin-1.

Let us look more closely at this lens. Generally accepted, that Rubin-1 (more precise Рубин-1Ц this means central or leaf shutter in Russian) is just a copy of the Voigtländer Zoomar, released in 1959. It is not true. These two lenses have the same principles but different design. The Rubin was designed by GOI (State Optical Institute in Leningrad) under the leadership of the famous Soviet optical designer David Volosov. He recognises that Zoomar was used as the basis and discusses it in his book ‘Photographic Optic’ issued by Искусство (The Art) publishing house in 1978. The Soviet lens was redesigned: as you can see, its glass elements are composed in a completely different layout compared to the Zoomar:

The Rubin barrel differs from the Zoomar in a striking fashion. Instead of push-pull zoom lever, the Soviet lens uses an ordinary rotating ring. Moreover, this optical device from Krasnogorsk is heavier and more bulky than its German counterpart.

Why did Volosov use the Zoomar as the prototype for the Rubin when, in the early 1960s, when there already many zoom lenses being produced over the world? He gives the reason in his book, giving comparative tables (pp. 376, 379). Optical design was developing extremely fast during those years and most of the new lenses were far better than the Zoomar.

My answer to this is only an assumption. One reason must be a very special design used in the Zoomar for matching the lens with the leaf-shuttered “Bessamatic System” applied in the Zenit-4 family. This system, named after the first Voigtländer Bessamatic model was used in many SLRs all over the world equipped with a behind-the-lens leaf shutter and interchangeable lenses.

The zoom lens era started when powerful computers appeared

To prevent vignetting, the exit pupil of all interchangeable lenses for such cameras must be as narrow as possible and close to the shutter leaves. The Zoomar was already designed to meet these requirements and good enough for the Zenit-4 family. The second reason could be the absence of modern computers in the USSR. The zoom lens era started when powerful computers appeared, because hand-made calculations did not allow for the design of such complex multi-lens optical systems.

Under these conditions, it was far more realistic for designers to recalculate an existing and verified design. It cannot be ruled out the opposite situation too; the decision to develop a leaf-shuttered SLRs was made to provide the Rubin lens with a matching camera. We’ll never know which is true.

It’s worth reminding readers, that the Zoomar was not even the first zoom lens in history. The first Cooke zoom lenses were released in the early 1930s for motion picture cameras. They partially replaced the dolly in cinema production and were sometimes used as additional method of expression. For still photography, however, zoom lenses were considered unusable. Precise cropping of pictures was always available in the darkroom.

But the worst thing was the dimensions and weight of these early zooms, even for smaller film formats like Academic 16x22mm. The standard photographic 35mm frame is more than twice as large: 24×36 mm. Movie zooms of that era were so bulky that they could not be used without a heavy tripod. Imagine the equivalent zoom for the larger frame!

The revolution finally happened in the late 1950s when electronic computers were created and the necessary calculations were simplified. The Voigtländer Zoomar appeared compact and lightweight enough to be attached onto a 35mm SLR. The new lens was convenient for shooting slides, which cannot be cropped in post processing. Nowadays, we might stop short of calling the Zoomar and especially the Rubin-1 “compact”. But note, they both have f/2.8 speed and were made more than 50 years ago.

My daily-carry Canon EF 24-105 IS USM looks equal to the Rubin, although it has a maximum speed only f/4.0. It’s just an ordinary lens, and the Zenit-6 with the Rubin attached is not bigger than my usual Canon EOS-1D series DSLRs.

But collectors have to keep a wider shelf for this set-up, almost as much as you would for a Hasselblad or Kiev-88.

Of course, I could not avoid the temptation to shoot at least one roll of film through this lens. My dream not inspired by the old black-and-white comedy ‘Zigzag of Luck’, the personal reason is different.

The first time I saw this camera and lens in the hands of my first photographic teacher. He showed it to me as expensive curio, already completely unusable for commercial photography in the late 1980s. But that first impression about this technical miracle lingered. It was the first-ever zoom lens for still photography, which I was able to touch with my own hands. At that time, foreign zoom lenses were not available in my city.

Two rolls of Fomapan 100 were immediately exposed. The Rubin was designed for reportage photography, my profession, so I took it to capture an event which was not part of that day’s news agenda – the communist meeting dedicated to May Day. It was the perfect setting to test the first Soviet photo zoom in a real “combat situation”.

The Zenit-4 with a Rubin-1 attached is weighty, but this heaviness is very pleasant. Of course, you need to get used to controlling it. The hand continuously attempts to rotate the zoom ring instead of focusing. The wide lens barrel definitely shades selenium light meter cell and you never cannot be sure what the needle in the viewfinder exactly shows: sky brightness or real exposure value. I set the fastest shutter speed of 1/500 to shoot at wider apertures because the Rubin’s automatic iris (by the way, the first ever in USSR too) does not have any depth of field preview.

Moreover, I was interested how this zoom answers to the most difficult optical challenge. The results were not impressive. I don’t know what is the reason, lens design quality or shoddy manufacturing of this particular example. But even closed to f/5.6~8 Rubin did not show acceptable sharpness in the corners of the frame. The closest shooting distance is 1.3m (4.3ft) and even at 80mm focal length you can make only a shoulder portrait.

I must say here, that the Rubin was for a long time the only photographic zoom lens available in the USSR. The Soviet lens market was quite poor and did not spoil the domestic photographers with a wide choice of equipment. My first zoom in 1993 was Soviet “Vario-Zenitar” 25~45 mm and it was full of aberrations. So, I’m not exactly surprised by the Rubin’s quality.

I would not recommend this lens for adaptation for modern mirrorless digital cameras. In addition to its poor optical quality, the Rubin would require complex engineering to create an  adaptor, because the automatic iris doesn’t have an adjustment ring on the barrel; the aperture values are set on the camera.

Instead of practical use with a Zenit-6, the Rubin-1 is one of the most attractive exhibit on any shelf. I never saw a Bessamatic camera in real life, but the tough and brutal lines of Zenit-6 are more pleasant for me than a sleek German profile.

It’s a pity that the leaf-shuttered family of Zenit did not survive more than four years of production. It could be have been a strong alternative to the Zenit-E family.

items.title: Harman Technology releases special football editions of popular black-and-white films – just in time for the World Cup
items.content:
British film producer Harman Technology is celebrating this summer’s football world cup with limited editions of two of its most popular Ilford Photo films.

The football-themed films feature images on the film box taken by sports photographer Miles Myerscough-Harris, who runs the @expiredfilmclub Instagram channel and has built up a huge following shooting sporting events on expired film.

The two films featuring Myerscough-Harris’s photographs are Ilford Photo XP2 Super and Ilford Photo HP5, two of Harman Technology’s 400-ISO films. Ilford Photo XP2 Super is a chromogenic film which can be processed in C41 colour chemistry.

“A couple of years ago we released limited-edition retro packaging for our HP5 Plus and FP4 Plus films and the feedback from the community was fantastic. Film shooters by their very nature are collectors and wanted more,” said Giles Branthwaite, the company’s sales and marketing director.

“With a World Cup around the corner, and as a company full of football (soccer) fans, we wanted to celebrate football fever by teaming up with Miles on this project,” he added.

The limited-edition films are available from Wednesday (27 May). The FIFA World Cup 2026, meanwhile, kicks off on 11 June.

The football-themed films are the last releases in a very busy year for Harman Technology, which in the past 12 months has released its budget-focused Kentmere 200 black-and-white film, a second version of its Phoenix 200 colour negative film and the second of its experimental colour films, Switch Azure.

It has also released its popular landscape and fine-art film, Pan F Plus, in large format for the first time.

items.title: One-off WWII Leica rifle camera for sale in June’s Leitz Photographica Auction
items.content:
A one-off Leica rifle camera built for use by the German Luftwaffe in World War II is one of the items on sale at the latest Leitz Photographica Auction in Germany in June.

The outfit was built as an extremely stable support for a 300mm lens for reconnaissance use.

The Astro Berlin rifle camera was designed around a Leica IIIc rangefinder camera, and the example being sold – believed to be the only one ever produced – includes a rare olive-green Leica IIIc finished in green paint.

Leitz Photographica Auction said: “The only known example of the Astro Berlin camera stock developed for the German Luftwaffe. This unique outfit was designed for handheld and tripod operation, the construction is lightweight and includes two wood handles, a left-hand shutter release and a padded rest for the face for maximal stability.

“The lens (Astro Fernbildlinse 5/300mm no.38912) and the viewfinder are painted in olive green, the cradle and tripod mount in grey. The rifle is paired with an unusual Luftwaffen Leica IIIc no.390415, finished in green paint, in a similar shade to the lens, it is also one of the latest Luftwaffen-Eigentum cameras listed in the Leica Archives.”

The camera has a starting bid of €60,000 (£51,800/$69,600)and is expected to sell for between €120,000 and €140,000 (£103,600-£120,900/$139,300-162,500).

The Astro Berlin rifle camera is one of a number of military cameras on offer at this summer’s sale, alongside prototypes, space cameras, and rare Soviet photographica. Kosmo will feature more of these lots in forthcoming posts.

The sale takes place in Wetzlar, Germany on Saturday 13 June.

items.title: Kosmo Foto Direktor now available in the Kosmo Foto Shop
items.content:
We brought something special along to London’s Photographica camera fair this week.

Fresh from a long day stickering and cainstering with the help of Chroma Camera‘s Steve Lloyd, we brought launched our first batch of Kosmo Foto Direktor 35mm film.

Direktor is re-rolled Double-X made by Eastman Kodak – a black-and-white cinema film used in movies such as ‘Raging Bull’, ‘Casino Royale’ and ‘Oppenheimer’. It’s our first special-edition film and the first cinema film offered by Kosmo Foto.

We offered the film first of all to Photographica attendees, with the intention being to offer it next at a photowalk held in co-operation with The Photographers’ Gallery Bookshop on Saturday 23 May. We were going to then offer the remainder of the first batch of Direktor to online customers after that.

This walk now has to be postponed – the new date will be announced very soon via the Photographers’ Gallery – which means that we can, in fact, offer Kosmo Foto Direktor through the Kosmo Foto Shop as of now.

BUY KOSMO FOTO DIREKTOR

The film is available in strictly limited quantities – only 150 rolls are up for grabs. Customers can order up to six rolls – we’d like as many people as possible to try out this first batch.

Later in the summer, our plan is to offer a new version with some extra-special elements – but more on that later.

Note: the film has been professional bulk rolled, using recycled film cassettes and canisters. All cassettes used are either Fuji or Kodak, as these have superior light traps. All cassettes are metal only, so won’t leave scratches.

The cassettes are DX coded for the film’s native ISO of 250.

Our first rolls are still waiting to be developed, and we’ll be adding sample photos from the first rolls to the listing, as well as publishing a “First Rolls” post.

items.title: The Other Photography Fair offers vintage photographica in London
items.content:
A new photography fair specialising in rare and collectable photographs from the 19th and 20th centuries is taking place in London for the first time this weekend.

The Other Photography Fair, which takes place amid the annual Photo London festival, has been organised by London auction house Chiswick Auctions.

The fair takes place from 8.30 on Saturday 16 May at the London Hilton Olympia.

“This fair is about reconnecting people with the physical and historical essence of photography,” said Austin Farahar, associate director and head of fine photographs at Chiswick Auctions. “In an increasingly digital world, there is something incredibly powerful about engaging with vintage photographic material, from the Daguerreotype to vintage silver gelatin prints, and all of the wonderful process and formats we can discover in between.

“We’ve created a space where both seasoned collectors and curious newcomers can discover, learn, and purchase incredible photography. There’s just an enormous breadth of fascinating material to discover under the umbrella of photographic art.”

Early bird entry (from 8.30am) costs £15 and normal entry (from 9.30am) costs £3.

The fair is intended to be a “satellite event during Photo London and offering an alternative, deeply focused experience for those passionate about photographic heritage and collecting”, a press release said.

“In addition to exhibitor stands, the fair will feature live demonstrations of early photographic processes, including Wet Plate Collodion, Cyanotype, Photogravure and Salt Paper printing workshops, giving visitors a rare chance to connect with historic photographic techniques.”

The fair is a day before the Photographic camera fair in London, the largest camera fair held in the UK.

items.title: Harman Technology releases large-format versions of Ilford Pan F Plus
items.content:
Harman Technology had announced the release of Ilford Pan F Plus black-and-white film in large-format sizes.

New versions of the fine-grained film – especially popular with landscape and fine-art photographers – are now available in in 4×5 and 8×10 formats.

Harman Technology said in a press release: “Renowned for its ultra-fine grain, exceptional sharpness, rich contrast, and beautiful tonal range, Ilford Pan F Plus has long been a favourite among photographers shooting landscapes, studio photography, portraits, and fashion. While the film has been available for decades in 35mm and 120 roll film formats, this marks the first time photographers can enjoy Pan F Plus in sheet film size.

“While the film has existed for many years in 35mm and 120 formats, a sheet film version has been on the wish list for film photographers for a long time,” said Giles Branthwaite, sales and marketing director at Harman Technology. “In fact, it is possibly the single most requested product we have, so I’m delighted to say we have listened and we have finally been able to deliver this on behalf of the film photography community.”

The new versions of one of the British film producers’ classic emulsions comes amid a burst of activity, much of it involving a recent shift into colour films.

Since the end of 2023, Harman Technology has pivoted into colour film for the first time. The original version of Harman Phoenix 200 colour negative film was followed by an improved follow-up, Phoenix II, in the summer of 2025.

It has since released experimental films with pronounced colour tints – the redscale Red in 2025, and the turquoise-toned Switch Azure earlier this year.

The company also recently published a video on YouTube showing the R&D behind new films and its hopes for the future of colour film development.

items.title: Introducing Kosmo Foto’s new film – Direktor
items.content:
In 2017 film photography blog Kosmo Foto launched its Space Age-themed Mono film.

In 2021, it went full film noir with its spy-themed film Agent Shadow.

Now, we’ve launched a third – one that you can’t buy in the shops, or even from the Kosmo Foto website.

Kosmo Foto Direktor is a limited-edition bulk-rolled version of Eastman Kodak’s much-loved 5222 XX black-and-white cinema film.

It’s a fantastic mono film that was purpose-built to be used in dim light. You’ll have seen it in films from ‘Raging Bull’ to ‘Casino Royal’ and ‘Oppenheimer’.

It has an ISO of 250 but can be pushed far beyond that and still yield fantastic results.

Direktor is our first bulk-rolled film, using recycled cassettes and canisters. It features a fantastic sticker design from My Mate Does Art evoking Soviet avant-garde cinema of the 1920s. Direktor will cost only £9.50 per 36-frame roll

It is being launched with a special early version “director’s cut” which will be available only at the Photographica camera fair in London on Sunday 17 May.

There will be fewer than 250 rolls available on the day – and once they’re sold, that’s it.

We are also keeping a very limited amount of stock for a walk in collaboration with The Photographers’ Gallery Bookshop. The Direktor walk will take place on Saturday 23 May, starting at The Photographers’ Gallery on Ramilles Street.

After that, the film is expected to be offered through the Kosmo Foto online store later in the summer. This version is likely to be different and even more collectable. We’ll be offering people the chance to pre-order it ahead of its production. The next batch is likely to be only 500 rolls – but if its popular we’ll announce more.

Direktor is one of a number of small-scale film releases Kosmo Foto has planned for the coming months – stay tuned for more.

items.title: Eastman Kodak adds large format and bulk films to new film range
items.content:
Eastman Kodak has announced large-format films and bulks rolls are now available new line-up of emulsions it distributes.

The announcement comes after the gradual release of all Kodak-branded 35mm and 120 films in new packaging – and sometimes new names – since last October.

The Kodak.com website now features a new promotion – titled “Time to go big” – on its Still Film section, where it announces all the new films. It also includes details of those films available in 100ft (30m) bulk rolls in 35mm.

Eastman Kodak said the new line-up of large format and bulk films is:

  • KODAK EKTAPAN 100 & 400 in 4X5 and 100-ft rolls
  • KODAK EKTACOLOR PRO 160 & 400 in 4X5 and 8X10
  • KODAK EKTAPAN 100 & 400 in 4X5
  • KODAK TRI-X 320 in 4X5, 5X7 and 8X10
  • KODAK TRI-X 400 in 100-ft rolls

“Look for the new box and you’ll know you’ve found us,” it said.

The announcement marks the end of Eastman Kodak’s roll-out of films to in-house distribution, some 14 years after it was outsourced to Kodak Alaris in the wake of the film-maker’s 2012 bankruptcy protection.

The new Eastman Kodak-distributed films do not include Portra or TMax films, as these brand names are currently owned by Kodak Alaris. Portra films are now known as Ektacolor Pro, and TMax films as Ektapan.

Kodak Alaris continues to offer some Kodak film under its own recently updated packaging. It currently offers large-format version of Ektachrome slide film and Ektar 100 colour negative film, which are not currently offered in the new Eastman Kodak range.
